title: The one dear to me (12.13–12.20)
hook: Krishna ends the chapter on devotion with a portrait, not a ritual
carry: free from hate, friendly to all

segments.voice: Yesterday: the ladder of practice. Fix your mind; if you can't, practice; if you can't, work as offering; if you can't, let go of the fruit. Did you take a smaller rung? Day two hundred three.

You probably know one person like this. The friend who doesn't hold grudges. Who's the same at a wedding and a hospital. Who doesn't need you to agree with them. You leave their kitchen lighter than you came in, and you're never quite sure how they do it. Chapter twelve is the chapter of bhakti, devotion. You might expect it to end with instructions: which offering, which mantra, how many times. It doesn't. It ends with a portrait of a person. Eight verses, and a refrain that keeps coming back.
screen: `THE FRIEND WHO HOLDS NO GRUDGES.` → `NOT A RITUAL.` → `A PORTRAIT.`

segments.voice: Verse thirteen opens the portrait. The one who hates no being, who is friendly and compassionate, free of mine and free of ego, the same in pleasure and pain, forgiving. In Sanskrit it starts adveshta sarva-bhutanam: without hatred toward all beings. Then maitra, friendly, a relative of the word for friend, and karuna, compassion. And each verse closes with some version of the same small phrase: sa me priyah. That one is dear to me. It's Krishna's voice, and it's tender. Verse fifteen is the one people repeat to each other. The one from whom the world does not shrink, and who does not shrink from the world. Nobody is afraid of them, and they aren't afraid of anybody. Then the portrait keeps going. Not elated, not hating, not grieving, not craving. The same to friend and enemy, in honor and in insult, in cold and in heat. Quiet. Content with whatever comes. And a surprising word in verse nineteen: aniketa, without a fixed home. Commentators read it as someone who doesn't cling to their house as the center of the universe, not necessarily someone homeless. Notice what isn't on the list. No rank. No caste. No particular ritual. The whole chapter on devotion ends by describing how a devoted person treats everyone else. Verse twenty closes the chapter: those who follow this with faith are exceedingly dear. That's the word today: the one dear to me. And that closes the chapter, and the week. We started with the vision that shook Arjuna, and we end with a kind face.
screen: `HATING NO BEING.` · `NO ONE AFRAID OF THEM.` · `THE SAME IN HONOR AND INSULT.` · `THAT ONE IS DEAR TO ME.` · then, large: `THE ONE DEAR TO ME.`

segments.voice: Sit, and bring to mind someone easy to love. Let yourself feel friendly toward them. Now someone neutral: a cashier, a neighbor you barely know. Offer them the same friendliness. Then, if you're willing, someone difficult. You don't have to fix anything. Just see if, for one breath, you can drop the hate and leave the friendliness. If that's too much today, go back to the easy one. The bell holds the time.
The one dear to me. Gita twelve, thirteen to twenty: a portrait of the devoted person, free of hate, friendly and kind, and the refrain, that one is dear to me.
screen: `THE ONE DEAR TO ME — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: free from hate, friendly to all. That's the week: the vision in chapter eleven, form or formless, the ladder, and the portrait. Today, let one person leave you lighter than they came. Day two hundred three.

screen: `DAY 203 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE BODY IS THE FIELD.`

howItsDone: Many Hindus memorize or recite Gita chapter twelve, the chapter of bhakti, because it is short; its closing verses (12.13–12.20) are often read as a description of the devotee's character.

myth: the chapter on devotion ends with a list of rituals
it ends with a portrait of a person: free of hate, friendly, the same in honor and insult.
verse 15 says no one is afraid of this person, and they aren't afraid of anyone
the world doesn't shrink from them, and they don't shrink from the world.
aniketa in verse 19 must mean a homeless wanderer
commentators often read it as not clinging to one's home, not necessarily having none.

fork.setup: you've reached the end of the chapter on devotion. what does Krishna finish with?
options: the right offerings and their times.
a portrait of how the devoted person treats everyone.
a warning to those who don't worship.
fork.reveal: a portrait. eight verses on character, each ending 'that one is dear to me'.

original.note: Sanskrit: priya, dear, beloved; the refrain 'sa me priyah', that one is dear to me.

trapdoor: what you thought: devotion means how much worship you do.
what it means: in Gita 12 devotion ends in character: free of hate, friendly, the same in praise and insult.
what a scholar hears: 12.13 opens 'adveshta sarva-bhutanam maitrah karuna eva ca'; the refrain 'sa me priyah' recurs through 12.20.
